content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
4	
5	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
8	
9	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
10	
11	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.
12	
13	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
14	
15	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.
16	
17	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
18	
19	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.
20	
21	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.
22	
23	The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.
24	
25	The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.
26	
27	The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.
28	
29	Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.
30	
31	FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

Source ledger result: the application text (title, cross-reference, government support, field, summary, brief description of drawings, detailed description, claims 1-20, abstract) traces cleanly to the inventor disclosure, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER passage in input/conversation.md. Every numbered part 10-66 in numerals.md corresponds to a part the inventor named ("cylindrical housing", "inlet", "outlet", "metering sleeve", "cylindrical dose chamber", "radial concentrate port", "carrier-liquid admission port", "flush bypass", "piston", "two axially spaced sealing lands", "reduced-diameter waist", "piston rod", "one-way outlet valve", "index collar", "helical cam groove", "follower pin", "three selectable axial stop faces", "spring-biased detent", "three recesses", "transparent window", "three reference numerals" (renamed "dose setting numerals"), "flexible lip", "flush poppet", "annular rinse channel", "two radial rinse openings", "replaceable cartridge", "threaded end cap"). Each numeral has one meaning; no numeral is used for two parts; every numeral in the table appears in the description; each figure's numeral list matches the parts the description attributes to that figure (FIG. 1: 10,12,14,16,18,52,64,66; FIG. 2: 18,20,22,24,30,32,34,38; FIG. 3: 22,26,28,44,56,58,60,62; FIG. 4: 36,40,42,44,46,48,50,54). Claim limitations all trace: the ordered isolation (claims 1, 5, 13), the rinse loop and its timing (claims 1, 4, 13, 16), the two directed rinse openings (claims 2, 15), the flexible-lip wipe preceding poppet opening (claims 3, 14), the indexing collar and cam groove (claims 6, 17), the three stop faces / detent / window numerals (claims 7-9, 18-19), and the cartridge and threaded end cap (claims 10-11, 20). Antecedent basis is sound throughout; the abstract is 145 words; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, or unresolved alternative remains in any file; no application-text sentence adds an "by way of example" or "any outline" embodiment to justify a drawing choice. Section-line designations are not implicated, since no figure is taken along a designated line and FIGS. 2-3 are enlargements of FIG. 1 rather than sections through a designated plane. Background prior-art characterizations were not assessed for inventor support, per instruction.

Three items need correction before render, all confined to the figure briefs:

1. FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass as an unobstructed passage running from the bore up through the upper sleeve band to the outlet, and separately places the normally closed flush poppet in a side branch at the opposite (left) end "joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage". As drawn, closing the poppet leaves the bore-to-outlet bypass path open, so the poppet gates nothing. That contradicts the description ("The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26... the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows...") and claim 1's whereby clause, which make flow through the flush bypass conditional on the follower pin opening the poppet.

2. FIG. 4 verbalizes an axial relationship between the index collar and the metering sleeve that no source passage supplies: "The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end." The inventor says only that "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." The overhang is load-bearing technical substance (it is what lets a pin on the rod end reach the groove without passing through the sleeve wall), and it is also in tension with FIG. 1, where the same ring is drawn "over the left portion of [the sleeve's] length" with the sleeve "standing in the left mouth and retained there by the end cap ring". The brief disclaims other undisclosed geometry (groove hand and pitch, which end carries the stop faces, the abutting part) but not this one.

3. FIG. 1 targets numeral 64 (cartridge) with an arrowed lead line landing on the metering sleeve's left end face, while numeral 18 (metering sleeve) is targeted on the same part's hatched band. Two numerals then land on one component, risking a reading of 64 as the sleeve's end face rather than the removable unit.

Everything else in the figure briefs is either an affirmatively disclosed part or a properly disclaimed depiction convention: the section-plane note that no circumferential relationship among ports is intended, the omission of rinse openings from FIG. 2 and of the collar from FIG. 3, the flexible lip "shown without flare direction", the rinse openings with "any direction of discharge is not indicated", the schematic inlet/outlet stubs with the express note that their drawn position is a convention only, and the broken-off outer mouth of the carrier-liquid admission port so that what it opens into is not indicated. The relative axial location of the carrier-liquid admission port downstream of the concentrate port is an entailment of the disclosed geometry (the waist between the lands registers with the concentrate port, and the downstream land "uncovers" the admission port), so it is not reported.

findings.title: FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass as permanently open to the bore, so the normally closed flush poppet gates nothing
findings.where: figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullets 7 and 8 ("Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber..." and "Adjacent the left end of the sleeve..."); cf. draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶ beginning "The flush poppet 58 is normally closed" and draft/09-claims.md claim 1 final wherein clause
findings.detail: The brief draws two independent routes to the outlet: an unobstructed passage from the bore through the upper band ('the flush bypass'), and a separate closure element at the far left ('the flush poppet') merely 'joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage'. With the poppet closed, the bore still communicates with the outlet through the bypass, so the depicted topology cannot produce the described and claimed behaviour in which carrier liquid flows through the flush bypass only while the follower pin holds the poppet open. This is a flow-path/topology defect, not a shape convention, and it makes the drawing inconsistent with both the description and claim 1.
findings.evidence: FIG-3.md: "Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber, a passage leads from the bore up through the upper band toward the outlet: the flush bypass." and "...a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage." Claim 1: "a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass; ... wherein the follower pin opens the flush poppet during a return stroke of the piston toward the fill position, whereby carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel, through the at least one rinse opening and through the flush bypass to the outlet". Description: "The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows..." Source: "the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass. Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel ... and then through the flush bypass to the outlet."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete the bullet "Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber, a passage leads from the bore up through the upper band toward the outlet: the flush bypass." and replace the following bullet with: "Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, where the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and standing between the bore and a plain passage that runs from it and opens through the upper band toward the outlet downstream of the dose chamber: the flush bypass, the passage having no other opening to the bore." findings.title: FIG. 4 asserts an untraced axial relationship in which the index collar overhangs the end of the metering sleeve

The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end, its hidden outline in broken line." Nearest source passage, which shows the gap: "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." No affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md or input/conversation.md describes the axial extent of the collar relative to the sleeve, or where the sleeve ends inside it.

The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end, its hidden outline in broken line." with: "its right end drawn with a shallow curved edge indicating the round section. Leave the rod, follower pin and groove bullets otherwise unchanged.

findings.detail: Numeral 18 is targeted on the metering sleeve's hatched upper band and numeral 64 is targeted, with an arrowed lead line, on the metering sleeve's left end face. Both lead lines therefore terminate on the metering sleeve, so numeral 64 can be read as designating the sleeve's end face rather than the removable cartridge as a unit. Description: "The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit."

Source ledger result: the application text (title, cross-reference, government support, field, summary, brief description of drawings, detailed description, claims 1-20, abstract) traces cleanly to the inventor disclosure, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER passage in input/conversation.md. Every numbered part 10-66 in numerals.md corresponds to a part the inventor named ("cylindrical housing", "inlet", "outlet", "metering sleeve", "cylindrical dose chamber", "radial concentrate port", "carrier-liquid admission port", "flush bypass", "piston", "two axially spaced sealing lands", "reduced-diameter waist", "piston rod", "one-way outlet valve", "index collar", "helical cam groove", "follower pin", "three selectable axial stop faces", "spring-biased detent", "three recesses", "transparent window", "three reference numerals" (renamed "dose setting numerals"), "flexible lip", "flush poppet", "annular rinse channel", "two radial rinse openings", "replaceable cartridge", "threaded end cap"). Each numeral has one meaning; no numeral is used for two parts; every numeral in the table appears in the description; each figure's numeral list matches the parts the description attributes to that figure (FIG. 1: 10,12,14,16,18,52,64,66; FIG. 2: 18,20,22,24,30,32,34,38; FIG. 3: 22,26,28,44,56,58,60,62; FIG. 4: 36,40,42,44,46,48,50,54). Claim limitations all trace: the ordered isolation (claims 1, 5, 13), the rinse loop and its timing (claims 1, 4, 13, 16), the two directed rinse openings (claims 2, 15), the flexible-lip wipe preceding poppet opening (claims 3, 14), the indexing collar and cam groove (claims 6, 17), the three stop faces / detent / window numerals (claims 7-9, 18-19), and the cartridge and threaded end cap (claims 10-11, 20). Antecedent basis is sound throughout; the abstract is 145 words; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, or unresolved alternative remains in any file; no application-text sentence adds an "by way of example" or "any outline" embodiment to justify a drawing choice. Section-line designations are not implicated, since no figure is taken along a designated line and FIGS. 2-3 are enlargements of FIG. 1 rather than sections through a designated plane. Background prior-art characterizations were not assessed for inventor support, per instruction.

Three items need correction before render, all confined to the figure briefs:

1. FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass as an unobstructed passage running from the bore up through the upper sleeve band to the outlet, and separately places the normally closed flush poppet in a side branch at the opposite (left) end "joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage". As drawn, closing the poppet leaves the bore-to-outlet bypass path open, so the poppet gates nothing. That contradicts the description ("The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26... the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows...") and claim 1's whereby clause, which make flow through the flush bypass conditional on the follower pin opening the poppet.

2. FIG. 4 verbalizes an axial relationship between the index collar and the metering sleeve that no source passage supplies: "The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end." The inventor says only that "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." The overhang is load-bearing technical substance (it is what lets a pin on the rod end reach the groove without passing through the sleeve wall), and it is also in tension with FIG. 1, where the same ring is drawn "over the left portion of [the sleeve's] length" with the sleeve "standing in the left mouth and retained there by the end cap ring". The brief disclaims other undisclosed geometry (groove hand and pitch, which end carries the stop faces, the abutting part) but not this one.

3. FIG. 1 targets numeral 64 (cartridge) with an arrowed lead line landing on the metering sleeve's left end face, while numeral 18 (metering sleeve) is targeted on the same part's hatched band. Two numerals then land on one component, risking a reading of 64 as the sleeve's end face rather than the removable unit.

Everything else in the figure briefs is either an affirmatively disclosed part or a properly disclaimed depiction convention: the section-plane note that no circumferential relationship among ports is intended, the omission of rinse openings from FIG. 2 and of the collar from FIG. 3, the flexible lip "shown without flare direction", the rinse openings with "any direction of discharge is not indicated", the schematic inlet/outlet stubs with the express note that their drawn position is a convention only, and the broken-off outer mouth of the carrier-liquid admission port so that what it opens into is not indicated. The relative axial location of the carrier-liquid admission port downstream of the concentrate port is an entailment of the disclosed geometry (the waist between the lands registers with the concentrate port, and the downstream land "uncovers" the admission port), so it is not reported.
